title: Great Zimbabwe and the Swahili Coast

cards.b:
In southern Africa, between about 1100 and 1450, people built a city of huge stone walls. They used no mortar. Each stone was shaped to fit, and the walls still stand.

Great Zimbabwe shows that African societies in the medieval world built large cities, long-distance trade and royal power, long before European explorers arrived.

The ancestors of the Shona people built Great Zimbabwe. The name means "houses of stone" in Shona. At its height it may have held many thousands of people, with farms and herds around it.

The Great Enclosure is the most famous part. Its outer wall rises up to about eleven metres in places, and the stones are arranged in fine courses. Inside were homes, a royal area and a mound where high-status people lived.

The city's wealth came from gold, which was mined in the area and traded to the coast. From the port towns of the Swahili coast, such as Sofala and Kilwa, it reached the Indian Ocean world.

Archaeologists have found Chinese porcelain and glass beads from the Indian Ocean at the site. They show that Great Zimbabwe was part of a long web of trade, not a cut-off place.

Peter Garlake (excavations, 1960s–1970s)

The British archaeologist Garlake dug at the site and studied its pottery, tools and building methods. He showed that the city was built by local people using local materials.

His work, published in Great Zimbabwe (1973), is a key source. It makes the African origin of the city clear.
The city was a capital for about three centuries. After it declined, the name lived on and gave a new country its name.

cards.h: The Swahili coast and its ships
cards.b:
Port towns on the East African coast, such as Kilwa, grew rich from the Indian Ocean trade. Arab, Persian and Indian merchants sailed there on the monsoon winds. The coastal people spoke Swahili, a language with many Arabic and Bantu roots.

Gold and ivory went out from the coast. Cloth, beads and luxury goods came in. The trade linked southern Africa to the wider world centuries before the Portuguese arrived.

cards.h: Did the Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba build it?
cards.b:
When European visitors first saw the ruins in the 1800s, many refused to believe that Africans had built them. Some claimed the Phoenicians, the Queen of Sheba or other outside peoples were responsible.

This idea was used by white settler governments to deny African achievement. Archaeology has shown the builders were Shona ancestors. Historians now treat the outside-builder theories as a myth with a political purpose.

Inside the ruins archaeologists found carved birds made of soapstone, a soft stone. Several have been found, and they look like a bird on a pillar. They may have been linked to religion or to kingship.

Today the bird is on Zimbabwe's national flag and coat of arms. The image shows how a site from the past can become a symbol of national identity in the present.

By about 1450 the great city had lost its people. Its farms and herds may have worn out the land. The trade may have shifted north along the coast and to other centres in the Limpopo basin.

Historians argue about the causes. Overgrazing, shifting trade, drought and political change are all possible. No single answer has been proved, and new evidence still changes the picture.

Gujarati merchants were among the traders on the monsoon routes to East Africa. They carried cotton cloth and beads, and their ships reached ports on the Swahili coast for many centuries.

The Indian Ocean was a single trade zone. Indian textiles, Chinese porcelain and African gold moved through the same network. Great Zimbabwe's wealth was tied to India as much as to the Mediterranean.

Five things to remember
  1. Great Zimbabwe was built by Shona ancestors between about 1100 and 1450.
  2. Its walls were built without mortar.
  3. Gold was traded to the Swahili coast and the Indian Ocean world.
  4. Colonial claims that outsiders built it were false.
  5. The Zimbabwe bird is on the national flag.
Think about it
  • Why do some societies deny the achievements of others?
  • What makes a ruin a symbol of nation?
